+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  DANCE — LANDSCAPE MAP                           |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                  |
|  WESTERN THEATRICAL DANCE                                        |
|  Ballet: court origins (1489+) → Romantic (1832) → Petipa       |
|          (1870-1903) → Balanchine neoclassicism → contemporary  |
|                                                                  |
|  Modern Dance: Duncan (1900s) → Graham (1920s+) →               |
|    Cunningham (1950s+) → Release technique → Post-Judson        |
|                                                                  |
|  Postmodern Dance: Judson Dance Theater (1962+)                  |
|    → Steve Paxton (contact improv) → Pina Bausch (Tanztheater)  |
|                                                                  |
|  NON-WESTERN CLASSICAL FORMS                                     |
|  Kathak (North India): ghungroo bells, footwork, spins          |
|  Bharatanatyam (South India): geometric, sculptural, mudra       |
|  Kathakali (Kerala): drama + extreme codified movement          |
|  Noh movement (Japan): extreme slowness, weight, ma (interval)  |
|  Beijing Opera movement (China): acrobatics + symbolic gesture  |
|                                                                  |
|  SOCIAL AND FOLK DANCE                                           |
|  (not covered here — vast; each culture, many forms)            |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

blocks.heading_context: ## Dance Notation — How Movement Is Written Down
blocks.text:
MOVEMENT NOTATION SYSTEMS
--------------------------
BENESH NOTATION (1955):
  Five-line staff (like music); the body represented
  on the staff; body positions notated in sequence.
  Used by the Royal Ballet and most classical ballet
  companies.

LABANOTATION (Rudolf Laban, 1928):
  More comprehensive than Benesh. Notates direction,
  level, duration, dynamic quality, body part used.
  Used for modern dance and ethnochoreological work.
  The staff is read from bottom to top (time moves up).

MOTIF NOTATION (Laban-based):
  Simpler than Labanotation; for less detailed purposes.

THE NOTATION PROBLEM:
  Dance notation is like programming: it describes
  a process that must be executed (embodied) to be
  real. The notation is not the dance, just as the
  score is not the music. The notation loses:
  - Exact dynamic quality
  - Individual performer's quality of movement
  - The feel of the space
  - What is NOT written (the between-movements transitions)

VIDEO/DIGITAL:
  Video documentation has mostly replaced notation
  as the primary preservation tool.
  But: video captures one viewpoint; it cannot capture
  the three-dimensional spatial design.
  Digital volumetric capture (motion capture) is
  the closest approximation to notational completeness.
  Motion capture in LIVE performance (distinct from archival):
  Markerless real-time tracking systems (e.g., Azure Kinect,
  OptiTrack) feed dancer position/pose data into generative
  visual engines (TouchDesigner, Notch). The dancer's movement
  drives real-time projected visuals, avatar puppeteering, or
  interactive scenography. The pipeline: camera → pose
  estimation → data mapping → visual render → projection,
  all at <30ms latency. This is a real-time computer vision
  + graphics pipeline where the dancer is the input device.
